one_liner: wasm2c translates a Wasm module to portable C; compiled natively, it outran Wasmtime, Wasmer and V8 on libsodium.
what_it_does: wasm2c (one tool in the WebAssembly Binary Toolkit) reads a .wasm binary and writes a C99 source file and header (C11 when the module uses threads/atomics). You compile that output with any C compiler together with the small runtime in wasm2c/wasm-rt-impl.c and wasm-rt-mem-impl.c, then call wasm2c_<mod>_instantiate() and the exported functions as plain C functions (w2c_<mod>_<export>(instance, ...)); imports are C functions the host must define. It is a build-time translator, not a runtime API like Wasmtime's or Wasmer's: no loading of modules at run time, no JIT.
how_it_is_fast: Ahead-of-time translation hands the whole module to an optimizing C compiler (clang or gcc at -O2/-O3, optionally -march=native and LTO), so the code gets the same register allocation, inlining and vectorization as native C. On 64-bit hosts linear memory is reserved with mmap and protected by guard pages, so most loads and stores need no explicit bounds check (an empty inline-asm FORCE_READ keeps the compiler from deleting loads that must trap); call_indirect uses a pointer-equality fast path on the function type before a cold slow path. An optional Segue mode (Linux/FreeBSD x86-64, clang 9+, -mfsgsbase, WASM_RT_ALLOW_SEGUE) keeps the linear-memory base in the %gs segment register.
when_to_use: Sandboxing a C/C++/Rust library inside a native host (the Firefox sandbox use case discussed in issue #2046) where you can add a build step and want near-native speed: 2.36x native geomean vs Wasmtime 3.46x on the 2022-12 libsodium suite.
CPU-bound modules known at build time (crypto, codecs, parsers) on x86-64 or aarch64 Linux/macOS where guard-page bounds checks are available.
Targets where a JIT is not allowed or no Wasm runtime exists but a C compiler does: the output is portable C99 with a small runtime.
When you want to reuse your existing C toolchain, sanitizers, profilers and debuggers on Wasm code.
when_not_to_use: Modules that arrive at run time (plugins, user uploads): every module needs a C compile, and wasm2c itself took about 1 minute (Ryzen 7950X) to over 3 minutes (Apple M3) on one Firefox build module (issue #2343).
When WAMR AOT is an option: in the same 2022-12 run iwasm AOT was at par (wasm2c used 1.03x iwasm's time geomean, slower on 31 of 61 tests).

Modules needing proposals the README table marks unsupported in wasm2c: relaxed-simd, function-references, wide-arithmetic (and GC, which is not in the table; issue #2348 'Plan for GC and beyond' is open).

Memory64 modules, 32-bit hosts, or builds that cannot install a SIGSEGV handler: wasm-rt.h falls back to explicit bounds checks (BOUNDS_CHECK), and on Windows or without the signal handler to stack-depth counting, which costs speed.
If you need a full runtime with WASI built in: the generated code expects the host to supply WASI imports (the Dhrystone example links uvwasi and libuv).

integration.dependencies: Generated code: libc and libm (pthreads for shared memory); WASI needs a host implementation such as uvwasi. The wasm2c tool itself: CMake 3.16+ build of WABT.
integration.min_toolchain: Generated code: C99 (C11 for threads/atomics); Segue needs clang 9+. Building WABT: C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20), CMake 3.16.
integration.platforms: Any C99 target; guard-page bounds checks need a 64-bit host with mmap and gcc/clang (or clang-cl since a 2026-09 commit); Segue only Linux/FreeBSD x86-64 with clang; big-endian (s390x) supported with stack counting.
integration.thread_safety: Module instances are separate structs; each extra host thread that runs Wasm code must call wasm_rt_init_thread()/wasm_rt_free_thread() (per-thread trap and stack state, after the race fixes tracked in issue #2046). Shared memories use a lock for memory.grow.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: runs the same .wasm modules as Wasmtime/Wasmer/V8, but replaces their runtime embedding API with generated C functions and a compile step; WASI and other imports must be provided by the host.

gotchas: Spec conformance at -O2/-O3 needs extra flags (wasm2c/README.md): GCC 11 '-fno-optimize-sibling-calls -frounding-math -fsignaling-nans', clang 14 '-fno-optimize-sibling-calls -frounding-math'; without them signalling NaNs survive, OOB-trapping dead loads can be deleted and infinite recursion may not trap (issue #1925). The repo's own Dhrystone/Segue benchmark Makefile compiles with plain -O3 and none of these flags, and the 2022-12 libsodium results do not say which flags were used.

The default build installs a SIGSEGV handler for guard-page traps and stack exhaustion; hosts with their own signal handling must coordinate or set WASM_RT_SKIP_SIGNAL_RECOVERY (then an OOB access may abort instead of trapping). Without the handler, stack depth counting traps at WASM_RT_MAX_CALL_STACK_DEPTH (default 500), which deep-recursive modules can hit.

Doc drift: wasm2c/README.md says 'cd wasm2c/benchmarks/segue && make', but the directory is wasm2c/benchmarks/dhrystone; the top-level proposal table leaves threads blank for wasm2c although wasm2c/README.md documents shared memories and atomics.

Benchmark caveats from the 2022-12 CSVs (recomputed this session): wasm2c was slower than Wasmtime on 2 of 61 tests (auth3 1.32x, keygen 1.43x) and recorded times below native on verify1 and sodium_utils, which points to run-to-run noise in this harness; the CSVs carry no unit, CPU, compiler or flags. The 2026 figures (0.814x Wasmtime, 0.887x Wasmer, search snippet of the blocked 00f.net post) used wide-arithmetic support the author added himself: the upstream README marks wide-arithmetic unsupported in wasm2c and no wasm2c wide-arithmetic PR by him appears in the repo.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick wasm2c over w2c2 when you want the spec-tracking reference translator (exceptions, tail calls, memory64, multi-memory, SIMD) maintained in the WebAssembly org with production use in Firefox; pick it over WAMR AOT or aWsm when you want plain C output you can build with your own compiler and toolchain rather than a separate AOT compiler, accepting that WAMR AOT matched it on libsodium.
verified_claims_summary: In Frank Denis's 2022-12 libsodium suite (61 tests, per-test times in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/2022-12/res), wasm2c output compiled natively took 0.68x Wasmtime's, 0.71x Wasmer Cranelift's, 0.82x Wasmer LLVM's and 0.61x Node/V8's time by geomean (derived from page data; 2.36x native vs Wasmtime 3.46x); CPU, C compiler and flags are not stated in the results repo, and the C compile step is not timed.
status_note: Actively maintained in the WebAssembly org (wasm2c fixes on 2026-09-16 and 2026-10-05), Apache-2.0; the generated C plus two runtime files are easy to vendor into any build.
